title: The Long Walk Home
summary: When their school bus breaks down far from the village, two classmates decide to walk the familiar road home together, helping each other and meeting a kind farmer along the way.
poll: It is better to wait for help than to walk home on your own.

versions.title: The Long Walk Home
versions.text:
Hind and Sara ride the bus home every day. The bus goes on a long road to their village.

One day, the bus stops. It will not go. The driver looks at it. He says, "This will take time."

Hind looks at the road. Their village is not too far. "We can walk," she says. "We know this road." Sara nods. They get off the bus.

The sun is hot. They walk and walk. Soon Sara is tired and thirsty. "I need to rest," she says. Hind holds her hand. "We will walk slowly," says Hind. "We will get home together."

They pass a small farm. A farmer sees the tired girls. He gives them cool water from a jug. "Thank you," says Hind. "Thank you so much," says Sara.

They walk on and feel better. At last, they see their village. They run home. Their mothers hug them. Hind and Sara tell them about the bus, the road, and the kind farmer.

versions.title: The Long Walk Home
versions.text:
Hind and Sara ride the bus home every day. The bus goes on a long, dusty road to their small village.

One afternoon, the bus suddenly stops. It will not start again. The driver checks the engine and shakes his head. "This will take a long time to fix," he tells the students.

Hind looks at the road ahead. Their village is not too far away. "We can walk home," she says. "We know this road well." Sara nods, and the two friends get off the bus.

The sun is hot, and the road is dusty. They walk and walk together. After a while, Sara feels tired and thirsty. "I need to rest a little," she says. Hind holds her hand and smiles. "We will walk slowly," says Hind. "We will get home together, step by step."

Soon they pass a small farm. A farmer is working near his trees. He sees the tired girls and waves. He gives them cool water from a jug and a few dates. "Thank you," says Hind. "Thank you so much," adds Sara.

Feeling better, the girls walk the rest of the way. At last, their village comes into view. They run the last steps. Their mothers hug them tightly. Hind and Sara tell them about the bus, the road, and the kind farmer.

One hot afternoon, the bus suddenly stopped in the middle of the road. It would not start again, no matter what the driver tried. He checked the engine, shook his head, and told the worried students, "This will take a long time to fix. I need to call the school for help."

Hind looked out at the familiar route ahead. Their village was not too far away, maybe three kilometers down the same road. "We can walk home," she said to Sara. "We know this road well, and it really is not that far." Sara hesitated, then nodded, and the two friends picked up their bags and stepped off the bus.

The sun felt hot, and the road was dusty beneath their shoes. They walked side by side, chatting about their school day to pass the time. After almost an hour, Sara began to feel exhausted and thirsty from the heat. "I need to rest a minute," she admitted quietly. Hind squeezed her hand and smiled. "We can walk slowly," Hind said kindly. "We will get home together, step by step."

Just then, they passed a small farm beside the road. A friendly farmer was working near his date palm trees, watering the soil. He noticed the two tired girls and waved them over kindly. He brought them cool water from a clay jug and some fresh dates to eat in the shade. "Thank you," said Hind happily, taking a long drink. "Thank you so much," added Sara, feeling grateful.

Feeling stronger after the short rest, the girls walked the rest of the way home, encouraging each other. At last, their village came into view in the distance. They ran the final steps, laughing with relief. Their mothers rushed out and hugged them tightly. Hind and Sara happily described the broken bus, the long road, and the kind farmer who had helped them home.

One especially hot afternoon, the bus suddenly stopped in the middle of the empty road. It would not start again, no matter what the driver tried. He checked the engine, shook his head, and told the worried students, "This will take a long time to fix. I need to call the school for help."

Hind looked out at the familiar route stretching ahead. Their village was not too far away, perhaps three kilometers down the same road they traveled each day. "We can walk home," she said to Sara with confidence. "We know this road well, and it really is not that far." Sara hesitated, glancing at the empty landscape, then nodded, and the two friends picked up their bags and stepped off the stranded bus.

The sun felt blazing hot, and the road was dusty beneath their shoes. They walked side by side, chatting about their school day to pass the time as the kilometers slowly went by. After almost an hour of walking, Sara began to feel exhausted and painfully thirsty from the heat. "I need to rest a minute," she admitted quietly. Hind squeezed her hand and smiled. "Thank you," said Hind happily, taking a long drink. "Thank you so much," added Sara, feeling truly grateful.

Feeling much stronger after the short rest, the girls continued home, encouraging each other and pointing out familiar landmarks. At last, their village came into view, its rooftops shimmering in the light. They ran the final steps, laughing with relief. Their mothers rushed out and hugged them tightly. Hind and Sara happily described the broken bus, the long road, and the kind farmer who had helped them home.

versions.title: The Long Walk Home
versions.text:
Every afternoon, Hind and Sara rode the school bus home, bumping along a dusty road that crossed the open desert toward their small village on the edge of the farmland, a journey so familiar that neither girl ordinarily gave it much thought.

One sweltering afternoon, the bus suddenly stopped in the middle of the empty road, its engine refusing to restart no matter what the increasingly frustrated driver tried. He finally climbed out, examined the engine, shook his head, and told the worried students that this repair would take a long time, since he needed to call the school for help on this isolated stretch of road.

Hind peered out at the familiar route stretching ahead and calculated that their village was not especially far away, perhaps three kilometers down that same road. She told Sara, with growing confidence, that they could simply walk home because they knew this road exceptionally well. Sara hesitated, glancing nervously at the parched landscape around them, then nodded, and the two friends gathered their bags and stepped off the stranded bus while the other students waited anxiously inside.

Although the sun felt scorching and the road was dusty beneath their shoes, the girls walked steadily side by side, chatting to pass the time as the kilometers slowly disappeared beneath their weary feet. After nearly an hour, Sara began to feel thoroughly exhausted and painfully parched from the heat. Hind, noticing her friend's struggle, squeezed her hand reassuringly and promised they would simply walk more slowly and still get home together, step by step, because that is what true friends are for.

Just then, they noticed a small farm beside the road, where a farmer named Abu Khalid was watering his thirsty soil with a practiced hand shaped by years of patient labor. He immediately noticed the two exhausted girls and waved them over with genuine hospitality. He brought them cool water from a clay jug along with sweet dates, gently insisting that these weary travelers rest a while in his shaded grove before continuing their journey. Both girls expressed their heartfelt gratitude for his completely unexpected kindness toward two tired strangers.

Feeling considerably stronger after that brief rest, the girls walked onward with real perseverance, encouraging one another while naming familiar landmarks they typically only recognized through the bus window. At last, their small village came into view, its rooftops shimmering brightly in the late afternoon light. The two girls ran the final steps together, laughing with genuine relief and quiet pride. Their mothers rushed outside, hugged them tightly, scolded them with gentle concern, and then pulled them close again. Hind and Sara happily recounted the broken bus, the parched road, and the kind farmer whose hospitality had helped them home.

versions.title: The Long Walk Home
versions.text:
Every single afternoon, Hind and Sara rode the school bus home together, bumping along a dusty road that crossed the open desert toward their small village on the edge of the farmland, a journey so utterly familiar that neither girl ordinarily gave it a second thought until the day everything unexpectedly changed for them both.

One sweltering afternoon, the bus suddenly stopped in the middle of the empty road, its engine sputtering noisily before falling completely silent, and no amount of effort from the increasingly frustrated driver could coax the stubborn vehicle back to life. He eventually climbed out, examined the engine thoroughly, shook his head, and informed the worried students that this particular repair would take a considerable amount of time, since he would need to telephone the school for assistance on this isolated, unpopulated stretch of road, far removed from any nearby town or passing traffic whatsoever.

Hind peered out at the familiar route stretching ahead across the sand and quickly calculated, in her head, that their village was not especially far away, perhaps three kilometers down that very same road they traveled daily without ever truly thinking about it, so she told Sara, with growing confidence while trying to sound considerably braver than she actually felt in that uncertain moment, that they could simply walk home because they knew this particular road exceptionally well. Sara hesitated for a long, uncertain moment, glancing nervously at the parched landscape surrounding them on every side, before finally nodding, and the two friends gathered their bags and stepped off the stranded bus together while the remaining students waited anxiously inside for some sign of rescue to eventually arrive.

Although the sun felt absolutely scorching overhead and the road was unbearably dusty beneath their worn shoes, the two girls walked steadily side by side, chatting to pass the time as the kilometers slowly disappeared beneath their increasingly weary feet, until, after nearly an entire hour of continuous walking across the open, shadeless terrain, Sara began to feel thoroughly exhausted and painfully parched from the unrelenting desert heat beating down without the slightest mercy anywhere in sight. Hind, noticing her friend's visible struggle immediately, squeezed her hand reassuringly while refusing to let her own quiet worry show on her face, and promised they could simply walk more slowly, repeating confidently that they would still get home together, step by step, because that, after all, is precisely what true friends are meant to do for one another, especially on a difficult day such as this one.

Just then, quite fortunately, they noticed a small farm beside the road, where its green date palms offered a genuinely welcome sight against the surrounding parched sand stretching endlessly beyond it in every conceivable direction. A farmer named Abu Khalid, who happened to be watering his thirsty soil with the kind of practiced hand that comes only from years of patient agricultural labor in that unforgiving climate, immediately noticed the two exhausted girls trudging past and waved them over with unmistakable, genuine hospitality, gently insisting that these weary travelers rest a while in his shaded grove, since the road itself was thoroughly unforgiving in such punishing heat, especially for young travelers far from any shelter. He generously brought them cool water from a clay jug along with a handful of sweet dates while they recovered their strength in the dappled shade his trees provided, and both girls expressed their heartfelt gratitude for his completely unexpected kindness toward two tired strangers passing along his farm that long, memorable afternoon.

Feeling considerably stronger after that brief but restorative rest, the girls walked onward with remarkable perseverance, encouraging one another the entire remaining distance while naming familiar landmarks they typically only recognized through the bus window each day of the school year. At last, when their small village finally came into view, its rooftops shimmering like a mirage finally made real after their lengthy ordeal, the two girls ran the final steps together, laughing with genuine relief and quiet pride at everything they had managed entirely on their own, without any adult guiding the way home safely. Their mothers rushed outside immediately, hugged them tightly, scolded them with gentle concern for worrying everyone so thoroughly, and then pulled them close once again in obvious relief that considerably outweighed any lingering frustration. Hind and Sara happily recounted the broken bus, the long parched road, and the remarkably kind farmer whose hospitality had helped them safely home that memorable afternoon.

wrong.B: The girls do not build a bus.
wrong.C: The farmer gives water; he does not sell it.
wrong.D: There is no race in the story.

questions.stem: Why do the girls get off the bus?
options: The bus is too crowded for them to stay
The bus stops and will not start again
The driver sends them to school on foot
They want to see the farmer's field
questions.why: The bus suddenly stops and will not start, so the driver says it will take a long time to fix.

wrong.A: The story never says the bus is crowded.
wrong.C: The driver wants to call for help, not send them to school.
wrong.D: They meet the farmer later, by chance.

questions.stem: Why does Hind think they can walk home?
options: She has a map of the desert, which shows the way home
She wants to pick dates on the way home from school
She knows the road well and it is not far
The driver tells her to walk, since the bus has stopped
questions.why: Hind says she knows the road and that the village is not too far away.

wrong.A: The story does not mention a map.
wrong.B: Picking dates is not her reason for walking.
wrong.D: The driver does not tell them to walk.

questions.stem: In the story, thirsty means —
options: feeling sleepy
feeling happy
walking very quickly down the road
needing something to drink
questions.why: Sara feels thirsty from the heat, which means she needs a drink.

wrong.A: Thirsty is about drinking, not sleeping.
wrong.B: Thirsty does not mean happy.
wrong.C: Thirsty is not about speed.

questions.stem: What does the farmer give the girls?
options: Cool water and dates
Bread and cheese
A ride on his donkey
New school bags
questions.why: The farmer brings them cool water from a jug and fresh dates.

wrong.B: The story does not mention bread.
wrong.C: The farmer does not give them a ride.
wrong.D: He gives water and dates, not bags.

questions.stem: Why does Hind hold Sara's hand on the road?
options: To play a game
To help her tired friend
To stop her from running off
To cross a busy street
questions.why: Sara is tired, so Hind holds her hand and says they will walk slowly together.

wrong.A: They are not playing a game.
wrong.C: Sara is not running away.
wrong.D: There is no busy street in this story.

questions.stem: What can you tell about the farmer from how he treats the girls?
options: He does not like visitors on his farm
He is too busy to help the girls
He is kind to strangers in need
He wants the girls to work for him
questions.why: The farmer notices the tired girls and kindly gives them water and food without being asked.

wrong.A: He welcomes them warmly.
wrong.B: He stops his work to help them.
wrong.D: The story never says he asks them to work.

questions.stem: Why does the author end with the mothers hugging the girls?
options: To show the mothers are angry
To explain how to fix a bus
To describe the farmer's house
To show how loved the girls are
questions.why: The warm hug shows the mothers' relief and love after the long walk.

wrong.A: The hug shows love, not lasting anger.
wrong.B: The ending is not about fixing buses.
wrong.C: The ending is about home, not the farm.

LOW.prompt: Would you have felt brave enough to walk home like Hind and Sara? Explain your answer using at least two details from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two details from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I think I would feel a little scared, but Hind and Sara show that walking together can make it easier. They know the road well, and they help each other when one of them gets tired. I would also feel better knowing a kind farmer might give me water, like he did for the girls.

keyWords.definition: the path or way a person travels from one place to another
keyWords.example: The bus driver knew a shorter route to school.
After the long hike, the hikers felt exhausted.
She was grateful when her neighbor helped carry the bags.

keyWords.definition: a cool, shadowy area out of direct sunlight
keyWords.example: We sat in the shade of the tree to cool off.

keyWords.definition: to give someone confidence or support
keyWords.example: Her coach tried to encourage her before the race.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: Two friends work together and receive kindness to get home safely after their bus breaks down.
A bus driver teaches two girls how to fix an engine.
A farmer in the area sells fresh dates and bottles of cool water to students walking by every single afternoon.
Two girls get lost in the desert and walk home alone.
questions.why: The story centers on Hind and Sara supporting each other and receiving help from a farmer as they walk home.

wrong.B: The driver does not teach them to fix engines.
wrong.C: The farmer gives dates; he does not sell them.
wrong.D: The girls know the road and are never truly lost.

questions.stem: About how far is the village from where the bus stops?
options: About thirty kilometers
About three kilometers
Less than one kilometer
The story does not say
questions.why: Hind thinks about the distance, and in the story, the village is perhaps three kilometers down the road.

wrong.A: Thirty kilometers is far too great a distance.
wrong.C: Less than one kilometer is too short.
wrong.D: The story does give an approximate distance.

questions.stem: What does the driver do when the bus will not start?
options: He decides to walk all the way home by himself instead of waiting
He asks the students to push the bus
He checks the engine and says he must call for help
He drives to the farm for water
questions.why: The driver examines the engine, shakes his head, and says he needs to call for help.

wrong.A: The driver does not leave the bus.
wrong.B: The story does not mention pushing the bus.
wrong.D: The driver does not drive anywhere.

questions.stem: Why does the farmer most likely offer the girls water and dates?
options: He wants them to work for him on his farm every single day after school
He is selling food along the road
He mistakes them for his relatives
He notices they are exhausted and wants to help
questions.why: He sees the two exhausted girls and kindly offers rest, water, and dates without asking for anything.

wrong.A: He never asks them to work.
wrong.B: He gives the food freely; he is not selling it.
wrong.C: Nothing suggests he mistakes them for relatives.

questions.stem: In the story, the word route means —
options: the path or way a person travels
a kind of fruit
a type of school bus
a special tool that farmers use in their fields
questions.why: The route is the familiar path the bus and the girls travel between school and the village.

wrong.B: Route is not a fruit.
wrong.C: Route describes a path, not a vehicle.
wrong.D: Route is not a farming tool.

questions.stem: Why does Hind tell Sara they will walk slowly and get home together?
options: To make the walk take longer on purpose
To encourage her tired friend
Because she does not know the way
Because the farmer told her to
questions.why: Sara is struggling, so Hind's words are meant to comfort and encourage her.

wrong.A: Hind wants to help Sara, not waste time.
wrong.C: Hind clearly knows the road well.
wrong.D: The farmer has not appeared yet at this point.

questions.stem: What causes Sara to need a rest during the walk?
options: She trips and hurts her foot on a big rock in the sand
She is frightened by an animal that runs across the path
The heat and the long walk make her exhausted and thirsty
She forgets which way to go and stops to think about the road
questions.why: The story says Sara becomes exhausted and thirsty from the heat after walking for almost an hour.

wrong.A: The story does not mention Sara tripping.
wrong.B: No animal frightens Sara in the story.
wrong.D: Sara does not forget the way; Hind guides them.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the events of the story?
options: By comparing two villages, paragraph by paragraph, and their farms and roads
By listing facts about desert farming and the crops that grow in the sand
By describing the driver's whole life, from his childhood to the day of the trip
In the order events happen: the breakdown, the walk, the farmer, and arriving home
questions.why: The story follows a clear sequence, from the breakdown to the walk, the farmer, and the final arrival home.

wrong.A: The story does not compare two villages.
wrong.B: The story is a narrative, not a list of farming facts.
wrong.C: The driver's background is not described.

MID.prompt: Explain how Hind and Sara worked together to get home safely. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how the two girls helped each other.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Hind and Sara worked together the whole way home. When the bus broke down, Hind suggested they walk because she knew the route well. Later, when Sara felt exhausted and thirsty, Hind held her hand and said they would walk slowly and get home together. Because they supported each other, and a kind farmer gave them water and dates to rest, the two friends made it safely back to their village.

keyWords.example: The parched travelers were relieved to find a spring.

keyWords.definition: a friendly and generous welcome given to guests or strangers
keyWords.example: The family's hospitality made the visitors feel at home.

keyWords.definition: steady effort to keep trying despite difficulty
keyWords.example: It took real perseverance to finish the long race.

keyWords.definition: very tired, especially from hard effort
keyWords.example: The weary climbers finally reached the top of the hill.

keyWords.definition: a feeling of trust in one's own abilities or decisions
keyWords.example: She answered the question with confidence.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the story?
options: Two friends rely on perseverance, kindness, and hospitality to get home safely.
A bus driver is blamed for an accident on a dangerous road in the mountains
A farmer refuses to help two tired travelers passing his land at night
Two girls compete to see who can walk home the fastest along the road
questions.why: The story highlights the girls' mutual support, determination, and the farmer's hospitality as they overcome the stranded bus.

wrong.B: No accident or blame appears in the story.
wrong.C: The farmer offers generous hospitality, not refusal.
wrong.D: The girls walk together rather than competing.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe Sara hesitating and glancing at the parched landscape before agreeing to walk?
options: To suggest she is uninterested in getting home
To show her genuine worry balanced against her trust in Hind
To reveal that she has strongly disliked Hind for quite some time
To explain why the bus engine failed
questions.why: Her hesitation and nervous glance reveal real uncertainty, yet she still nods and goes, trusting her friend.

wrong.A: She clearly wants to get home, which is why she agrees.
wrong.C: Nothing suggests she dislikes Hind; she trusts her.
wrong.D: Her hesitation is not connected to the engine failure.

questions.stem: How does Abu Khalid's hospitality affect the girls' journey?
options: It delays them so much that they never reach the village
It convinces them to stay on the farm permanently with him and work there
It gives them rest, water, and renewed strength to finish the walk
It causes them to take a different road to the village
questions.why: After resting and drinking water at the farm, the girls feel stronger and continue walking with real perseverance.

wrong.A: The brief rest does not stop them from reaching home.
wrong.B: The girls continue on toward their village, not the farm.
wrong.D: They continue on the same road after resting.

questions.stem: In the story, the word hospitality means —
options: a type of medicine given to sick travelers
a formal rule about crossing someone's land
a rare and unusual type of desert plant found only in remote oases
a friendly and generous welcome given to guests or strangers
questions.why: Abu Khalid's hospitality is shown through his generous, friendly welcome of the two tired strangers.

wrong.A: Hospitality is not a medicine.
wrong.B: The story does not describe a formal land rule.
wrong.C: Hospitality is not a plant.

questions.stem: What can readers infer about Hind from her decision to suggest walking home?
options: She is confident and willing to take responsibility for a plan
She is reckless and does not think about safety, so she makes a bad plan
She is afraid of the bus driver, and so she wants to walk home alone
She dislikes her classmates and wants to be alone on the long road
questions.why: Hind calmly assesses the distance, proposes a reasonable plan, and reassures Sara throughout, showing confidence.

wrong.B: She carefully judges the distance before deciding.
wrong.C: Nothing in the story suggests fear of the driver.
wrong.D: Hind clearly cares about her classmate, Sara.

questions.stem: In what order do these events occur in the story?
options: The girls reach the village, the bus stops, they meet the farmer, the girls decide to walk
The bus stops, the girls decide to walk, they meet the farmer, they reach the village
They meet the farmer, the bus stops, the girls decide to walk, they reach the village
The girls reach the village, they meet the farmer, the bus stops, the girls decide to walk
questions.why: The bus breaks down first, then the girls decide to walk, then they meet the farmer along the way, and finally they arrive home.

wrong.A: The village is reached last, not first.
wrong.C: The farmer is met after the bus stops, not before.
wrong.D: The bus stopping is the first event, not the last.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the detail that the mothers scold the girls gently before hugging them again?
options: To show the mothers do not trust the girls and are very angry
To suggest the girls will be punished for a whole week at home
To show that worry and relief can exist together in a loving family
To explain how far the village is from the school and the market in the town
questions.why: The gentle scolding followed by another hug shows the mothers' fear and love and relief can occur together.

wrong.A: The hug shows trust and affection, not distrust.
wrong.B: There is no mention of punishment.
wrong.D: This detail is about emotion, not distance.

questions.stem: Based on the story, what is the most likely reason Hind and Sara overcome the challenge of the broken bus?
options: They happen to find a working phone along the road and call their parents
The driver secretly fixes the engine and drives them the rest of the way
They decide to wait at the bus for the rest of the afternoon until the sun goes down
Their teamwork, calm thinking, and the farmer's hospitality together help them succeed
questions.why: The story shows that Hind's planning, the girls' mutual encouragement, and Abu Khalid's generosity all combine to get them home safely.

wrong.A: No phone is found along the road.
wrong.B: The bus never gets fixed in the story.
wrong.C: They choose to walk rather than wait.

HIGH.prompt: Do you think Hind and Sara made a good decision to walk home instead of waiting for the bus to be fixed? Support your argument with evidence from the story, and address a reason someone might disagree with you.
checklist: I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think Hind and Sara made a good decision to walk home. They knew the road well, the village was only about three kilometers away, and they supported each other the entire way, which shows real perseverance. They were also fortunate to meet Abu Khalid, whose hospitality gave them water and rest exactly when they needed it most. Someone might argue that walking alone in desert heat is risky and that waiting for help would have been safer, and that is a fair point. However, because the girls knew the route, stayed together, and found help along the way, their choice turned out to be both reasonable and successful.

LOW.stem: What does the bus driver say about the bus?
options: "It is a fast bus."
"This will take time."
"We are close to home."
"Please get on the bus."
LOW.why: In the story, the driver says the bus will take a long time to fix.

wrong.A: The bus is stopped, so he does not say it is fast.
wrong.C: Hind is the one who says the village is not far.
wrong.D: The girls get off the bus.

LOW.stem: Why does Sara need to rest?
options: She is tired and thirsty
She has lost her bag
She is afraid of the farm
She wants to read a book
LOW.why: The sun is hot, and Sara is tired and thirsty.

wrong.B: Her bag is not mentioned.
wrong.C: She is not afraid of the farm.
wrong.D: Reading is not mentioned.

LOW.stem: What happens right after the farmer gives the girls water?
options: They go back to the stopped bus
They run into the farm to play
They walk on, feeling better
They sit and fall asleep there
LOW.why: After the water, the girls walk on and feel better.

wrong.A: They keep walking toward the village.
wrong.B: The text does not say they play on the farm.
wrong.D: The text does not say they sleep.

LOW.stem: In the story, what does it mean when Sara "nods"?
options: She says no out loud
She falls fast asleep
She waves a long goodbye
She moves her head for yes
LOW.why: Hind says they can walk, and Sara nods and gets off the bus, so she is saying yes.

wrong.A: Sara gets off the bus, so she did not say no.
wrong.B: She is awake and walking.
wrong.C: She is not leaving; she is agreeing.

MID.stem: What food did the farmer give the girls with the water?
options: Fresh dates
Warm bread
Sweet rice
Dried fish
MID.why: The story says he gave them water and some fresh dates.

wrong.B: Bread is not mentioned.
wrong.C: Rice is not mentioned.
wrong.D: Fish is not mentioned.

MID.stem: In the story, the word hesitated means Sara —
options: jumped up with great joy
ran ahead of the others
paused, feeling unsure
fell asleep in the heat
MID.why: Sara hesitated and then nodded, which shows she paused before she agreed.

wrong.A: She nodded, but she did not jump for joy.
wrong.B: The girls walk side by side.
wrong.D: She is awake and then walks.

MID.stem: Why did the girls feel stronger after the short rest?
options: The bus came to pick them up
They had water and dates
The sun went away at last
Their bags became lighter
MID.why: The farmer gave them cool water and dates to eat in the shade.

wrong.A: The bus never comes in the story.
wrong.C: The sun stays hot.
wrong.D: Their bags are not mentioned.

MID.stem: The girls ran the last steps, "laughing with relief." What does this show?
options: They were still very afraid
They wanted to go back
They were angry at Hind
They were glad to be home
MID.why: Laughing with relief shows the girls were happy their hard walk was over.

wrong.A: Relief means the fear is gone.
wrong.B: They run toward their village.
wrong.C: Nothing in the story shows anger.

HIGH.stem: Where did Abu Khalid insist the girls rest?
options: In his shaded grove
Inside the stopped bus
Beside the dusty road
On top of a hill
HIGH.why: The story says he insisted the girls rest a while in his shaded grove.

wrong.B: The bus was far back on the road.
wrong.C: The farmer led them to the shade, away from the road.
wrong.D: No hill is mentioned.

HIGH.stem: In the story, the word parched most nearly means —
options: very wet
very dry
very loud
very green
HIGH.why: The landscape is parched and Sara feels parched from the heat, so it means very dry.

wrong.A: The road and desert are dry, not wet.
wrong.C: Parched does not describe sound.
wrong.D: The desert is dry, not green.

HIGH.stem: Why did Hind promise to walk more slowly?
options: She wanted to see the farm
The road was very short
Sara was exhausted
The bus was close behind
HIGH.why: Sara felt exhausted and parched, so Hind promised they would go more slowly together.

wrong.A: The farm appears later.
wrong.B: The village was about three kilometers away.
wrong.D: The bus stayed stranded.

HIGH.stem: The girls named landmarks they usually saw only from the bus window. What does this suggest?
options: They had walked this road many times
They had never seen these places at all
They had a map to guide them
Walking this road was new for them
HIGH.why: They normally saw the landmarks only through the bus window, so walking the road on foot was a new experience.

wrong.A: They usually rode the bus, so they had not walked it often.
wrong.B: They recognized the landmarks, so they had seen them before.
wrong.C: The story does not mention a map.
